title: Le gardien du musée
summary: The morning after an alarm, a night guard explains what he saw.

cast.name: Moi
cast.description: The narrator, "Moi": a learner in their 30s who lives in Paris. Friendly, relaxed, a bit self-mocking.
cast.label: ink-500

cast.name: Madame Delorme
cast.description: The director of a small Paris museum, a Parisian woman in her fifties. Brisk, no-nonsense, dry and sceptical but fair; crisp, precise speech.

cast.name: Raymond
cast.description: The museum’s night guard, an older Parisian man of 64. Sincere, earnest, a little shaken; tells his story warmly, with wide eyes.

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: Lundi, sept heures du matin. J’apportais les cafés à Madame Delorme, la directrice du musée.
story.en: Monday, seven in the morning. I was bringing the coffees to Madame Delorme, the museum’s director.

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: Raymond, le gardien de nuit, était assis devant son bureau, tout pâle.
story.en: Raymond, the night guard, was sitting in front of her desk, white as a sheet.

story.speaker: madame-delorme
story.fr: — L’alarme a sonné à trois heures, Raymond. Je vous écoute.
story.en: “The alarm went off at three, Raymond. I’m listening.”

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: — Pendant ma ronde, je me suis assis un moment devant le portrait de la Comtesse.
story.en: “During my round, I sat down for a moment in front of the portrait of the Countess.

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: Il faisait noir. J’ai entendu un craquement, alors je me suis caché derrière une sculpture.
story.en: It was dark. I heard a creak, so I hid behind a sculpture.”

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: Madame Delorme a levé un sourcil. Raymond a continué, à voix basse.
story.en: Madame Delorme raised an eyebrow. Raymond went on, in a low voice.

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: — Et là, la Comtesse s’est levée, et elle est sortie de son cadre !
story.en: “And then the Countess stood up, and she stepped out of her frame!

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: Elle s’est étiré les bras, comme après une longue nuit.
story.en: She stretched her arms, like after a long night.

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: On s’est regardés, mais on ne s’est pas parlé.
story.en: We looked at each other, but we didn’t speak.

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: Puis elle s’est assise dans le fauteuil des visiteurs… et l’alarme a sonné.
story.en: Then she sat down in the visitors’ armchair… and the alarm went off.”

story.speaker: raymond
story.fr: — Je ne me suis pas endormi ! Enfin… cinq minutes, mais avant tout ça.
story.en: “I did not fall asleep! Well… five minutes, but before all that.”

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: Alors elle a ouvert son ordinateur et lancé les images de la caméra de surveillance.
story.en: So she opened her laptop and played the security camera footage.

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: À trois heures, le cadre était vide, et le fauteuil des visiteurs était tourné.
story.en: At three o’clock, the frame was empty, and the visitors’ armchair had been turned.

story.speaker: narrator
story.fr: J’ai eu la chair de poule. Madame Delorme a refermé l’ordinateur, très lentement.
story.en: I got goosebumps. Madame Delorme closed the laptop again, very slowly.

story.speaker: madame-delorme
story.fr: — Raymond… on ne dit rien à personne.
story.en: “Raymond… we don’t say a word to anyone.”

notes.title: « Je me suis assis » : pourquoi « être » ?
notes.short: Reflexive verbs always form the passé composé with être, for every person.
body: Apps teach the être verbs as a list: aller, venir, partir… Add a second rule: every reflexive verb takes être, with no exceptions. Je me suis assis, tu t’es endormi, nous nous sommes cachés.
The pronoun stays glued in front of être: me, te, se, nous, vous, se.
Quick check: is there a me, te, se, nous or vous that points back to the subject? Then it’s être.

examples.fr: Je me suis assis un moment devant le portrait.
examples.en: I sat down for a moment in front of the portrait.

examples.fr: Nous nous sommes cachés derrière une statue.

notes.spoken: In speech, nous nous sommes becomes on s’est: « On s’est cachés derrière une statue. » And je me suis often blurs into « j’me suis » in fast speech.

trap.why: Avoir never goes with a reflexive verb. Once you have me, te or se, you need être.

notes.title: « La Comtesse s’est levée » : pourquoi un -e ?
notes.short: With reflexive verbs, the past participle usually agrees with the subject, like other être verbs.
body: The Countess is feminine, so levée takes an -e. Plurals add -s: ils se sont levés, elles se sont levées.
Strictly, it agrees with se, the direct object in front of the verb. But se is the same person as the subject, so in practice: match the subject.
That’s why Raymond, a man, says je me suis caché, while the Countess would say je me suis cachée.

examples.fr: Je me suis caché derrière une sculpture.

notes.spoken: Levé, levée and levés all sound the same, so you see this agreement far more than you hear it. The note on assise shows when you can hear it.

trap.why: The Countess is feminine, so the participle takes an -e, even though you can’t hear it.

notes.title: Pourquoi « on s’est regardés » mais « on ne s’est pas parlé » ?
notes.short: No agreement when se is an indirect object, or when a direct object comes after the verb.
body: Agreement follows the direct object. You look at someone (regarder quelqu’un), so se is the direct object and it agrees: on s’est regardés.
But you speak to someone (parler à quelqu’un): se means “to each other”, an indirect object, so no agreement. Same for se téléphoner, se dire, se sourire.
And in elle s’est étiré les bras, the direct object is les bras, after the verb: no agreement with elle.

examples.fr: On s’est regardés, mais on ne s’est pas parlé.
examples.en: We looked at each other, but we didn’t speak.

notes.spoken: These endings are silent, so you won’t hear the difference, and many French people get it wrong in writing. Get it right in an email and you’ll impress.

trap.why: You speak to someone (parler à), so se is indirect and the participle doesn’t agree.

notes.title: « Elle s’est assise » : ça s’entend ?
notes.short: When the participle ends in a silent consonant, the feminine -e makes it heard: assis, assise.
body: Most participles end in a vowel (levé, endormi), so the -e changes nothing out loud. A few end in a silent consonant: assis, mis, pris. The -e brings that consonant back.
Il s’est assis is said [asi]; elle s’est assise, [asiz]. When Raymond says assise, you know it’s the Countess who sat down, not him.
Same with mettre: elle s’est mise à rire, she started laughing.

examples.fr: Puis elle s’est assise dans le fauteuil.
examples.en: Then she sat down in the armchair.

examples.fr: Je me suis assis un moment.
examples.en: I sat down for a moment.

notes.spoken: A listening tip: a [z] at the end of the participle (assise, mise, prise) tells you the subject is feminine, even if you missed who it was.

trap.why: Say the [z]. Without it, a French ear pictures a man sitting down.

notes.title: « Je ne me suis pas endormi ! » : où va la négation ?
notes.short: Ne goes before the pronoun, and pas after être: the pronoun and être stay together.
body: The pronoun and être stick together, and the negation wraps around both: je ne me suis pas endormi, elle ne s’est pas levée.
Never put ne between them: not « je me ne suis pas ».
It works the same with the other negations from lesson 2: on ne s’est jamais parlé, il ne s’est rien passé.

examples.fr: Je ne me suis pas endormi !

notes.spoken: In speech the ne goes, as usual: « Je me suis pas endormi ! » Fast, it sounds like « j’me suis pas endormi ».

trap.wrong: Je me ne suis pas endormi.
trap.right: Je ne me suis pas endormi.
trap.why: Ne goes in front of the pronoun, never between the pronoun and être.

quiz.prompt: Listen to Raymond. What did he do when he heard a noise?

options.text: He switched on all the lights.
options.why: Nothing about lights: « il faisait noir », it was dark, and he stayed in the dark.
« Je me suis caché derrière une sculpture »: I hid behind a sculpture. Se cacher, with être.
He doesn’t call anyone. He hears « un craquement », a creak, and hides.

quiz.prompt: Listen to Raymond. What does he admit?

options.text: He slept through the whole night.
options.why: Not the whole night: « cinq minutes », only five minutes.

options.text: He set off the alarm by mistake.
options.why: He never says that. In his story, the alarm goes off when the Countess sits down.

options.text: He dozed for five minutes, but before it all happened.
options.why: « Enfin… cinq minutes, mais avant tout ça »: well, five minutes, but before all that.

quiz.quote: — Et là, la Comtesse s’est levée, et elle est sortie de son cadre !

options.text: The Countess is feminine, and the participle agrees with the subject.
options.why: Reflexive verbs take être, and the participle agrees: la Comtesse s’est levée, Raymond s’est levé.

options.text: Se lever always ends in -ée in the past.
options.why: Not always: a man says je me suis levé, with no extra -e. It depends on who gets up.

options.text: Levée is a noun here, like “la levée du courrier”.
options.why: It’s the verb se lever in the passé composé, after s’est. La levée is a different word.

quiz.quote: On s’est regardés, mais on ne s’est pas parlé.
quiz.prompt: Why “regardés” with an -s, but “parlé” with no ending?

options.text: You look at someone, but you speak to someone: only a direct object agrees.
options.why: Regarder quelqu’un: se is direct, so it agrees. Parler à quelqu’un: se is indirect, so no agreement.

options.text: Parlé is in the negative, and negatives never agree.
options.why: Negation has nothing to do with it: on s’est parlé, positive, doesn’t agree either.

options.text: Regarder uses être and parler uses avoir.
options.why: Both are reflexive here, so both use être: on s’est regardés, on ne s’est pas parlé.

quiz.quote: — Raymond… on ne dit rien à personne.
quiz.prompt: In “on ne dit rien à personne”, who is “on”?

options.why: On can mean people in general, but here she’s making a pact with the people in the room.
The Countess is on the video, not in the office. On is the people watching it.

options.text: Madame Delorme, Raymond and the narrator: “we”.
options.why: In speech on usually means nous. She means: none of us says anything.

quiz.quote: À trois heures, le cadre était vide, et le fauteuil des visiteurs était tourné.
quiz.prompt: Why does Madame Delorme close the laptop so slowly?

options.text: She’s angry that Raymond slept on duty.
options.why: If she were angry, she’d say so. Instead she asks everyone to keep quiet.

options.text: The footage shows the empty frame and the turned chair: Raymond may be telling the truth.
options.why: She was sure he’d dreamed it. The video says otherwise, and she isn’t ready to say it out loud.

options.text: The video is blank because the camera was broken.
options.why: The video works: it shows the frame, empty, and the armchair, turned.

phrases.note: « Que dalle » means nothing at all, very familiar. « Il faisait noir » is the everyday neutral version.

phrases.spoken: J’ai eu une de ces trouilles !
phrases.note: La trouille is fear, familiar. « J’ai eu la chair de poule » (goosebumps) works anywhere.

phrases.written: Je ne me suis pas endormi.
phrases.note: The ne drops in speech, and the pronoun and être stay together: me suis, never split.
What everyone says after something definitely happened. Rien carries the negation once ne is gone.

phrases.written: Nous ne dirons rien à personne.
phrases.note: On replaces nous, the present replaces the future, and the ne goes. Same promise, more conspiratorial.

phrases.written: Je me suis assoupi quelques instants.
phrases.spoken: J’ai piqué du nez cinq minutes.
phrases.note: Piquer du nez: your nose drops as you nod off. What Raymond would say to a friend, never to his director.

describe.alt: A pink museum gallery: a guard in a blue suit spreads his arms in front of a big blue sculpture while three dogs run across the chequered floor; a woman on a bench looks at her phone and a man looks at a painting
describe.caption: Le musée · un mardi, 10 h
describe.instructions: Write 3 to 5 sentences: what happened in the museum this morning? Who did what? Use reflexive verbs in the passé composé (ils se sont échappés, il s’est mis…).
describe.placeholder: Ce matin, trois chiens se sont…
helpers: ils se sont mis à courir
describe.scene: A flat, colourful illustration of a bright museum gallery with pink walls and a pink and white chequered floor. In the middle, a museum guard in a blue suit and burgundy tie, with a walkie-talkie on his jacket, spreads his arms wide and looks alarmed, protecting a large blue knotted sculpture on a white plinth behind him. Three dogs run past him: a black-and-white dalmatian with its tongue out, a small blue French bulldog with a yellow collar, and an orange-and-white long-eared dog with a green collar. On the left, a woman with pink hair sits on a pink bench looking at her phone, next to a potted plant, under an arched window showing green bushes. On the right, a man in a green jumper stands with his hands behind his back looking at a small abstract painting. On the back wall hangs a large framed painting of a green bird, and two blue pendant lamps hang from the ceiling.

sample.text: Ce matin, trois chiens se sont échappé et ils sont entrés dans le musée. Le gardien s’a mis devant la sculpture bleu. Une dame s’est assis sur un banc, mais elle regarde son téléphone. Un visiteur ne s’est retourné pas. Moi, je me suis bien amusée !

segments.t: Ce matin, trois chiens se sont
et ils sont entrés dans le musée. Le gardien
sur un banc, mais elle regarde son téléphone. Un visiteur
. Moi, je me suis bien amusée !

corrections.why: S’échapper takes être, and the subject is trois chiens, masculine plural: se sont échappés.
Reflexive verbs always take être, never avoir: il s’est mis devant la sculpture.
Sculpture is feminine, so the adjective takes an -e: la sculpture bleue.
The subject is une dame, so the participle takes an -e, and you can hear it: assise [asiz].
Ne and pas wrap around the pronoun and être, before the participle: il ne s’est pas retourné.

result.corrected: Ce matin, trois chiens se sont échappés et ils sont entrés dans le musée. Le gardien s’est mis devant la sculpture bleue. Une dame s’est assise sur un banc, mais elle regarde son téléphone. Un visiteur ne s’est pas retourné. Moi, je me suis bien amusée !
result.spoken: Ce matin, trois chiens se sont échappés et ils ont débarqué dans le musée. Le gardien s’est jeté devant la sculpture bleue. Y a une dame assise sur un banc, elle regarde son téléphone. Et un monsieur s’est même pas retourné. Franchement, je me suis bien marrée !
result.spokenNote: Débarquer (to burst in), se jeter (to throw yourself) and se marrer (to have a laugh) are everyday spoken verbs. Il y a becomes y a, and the ne disappears.

ambience.prompt: A small museum office early in the morning: the hum of a laptop, a radiator ticking, a wall clock, coffee cups set down on a wooden desk, distant footsteps echoing in an empty gallery, an old building creaking softly. Calm and steady. No music, no clear speech.
